---
title: "Working with ggplot2"
---

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 5,
  fig.height = 3.2,
  dpi = 120
)
# size each plot chunk from the plot itself (ggtargets::dag_size()), so
# nodes, lines and text look the same in every figure
knitr::opts_hooks$set(dag_fig = function(options) {
  code <- paste(options$code, collapse = "\n")
  if (!isTRUE(options$eval) || !grepl("ggplot_dag|tar_ggplot", code)) {
    return(options)
  }
  seed <- if (exists(".Random.seed", globalenv())) {
    get(".Random.seed", globalenv())
  }
  wd <- getwd()
  on.exit({
    setwd(wd)
    if (is.null(seed)) {
      suppressWarnings(rm(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()))
    } else {
      assign(".Random.seed", seed, globalenv())
    }
  })
  root <- knitr::opts_knit$get("root.dir")
  if (!is.null(root)) {
    setwd(root)
  }
  size <- tryCatch(
    {
      p <- eval(parse(text = code), new.env(parent = knitr::knit_global()))
      if (ggplot2::is_ggplot(p) && !inherits(p, "patchwork")) {
        ggtargets::dag_size(p)
      }
    },
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(size)) {
    options$fig.width <- size[["width"]]
    options$fig.height <- size[["height"]]
  }
  options
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dag_fig = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggtargets)
library(ggplot2)
```

`ggplot_dag()` returns a plain `ggplot` object, and `dag_layers()` a plain list of layers - both compose with the rest of ggplot2 like any other plot.

```{r}
#| label: dag
dag <- as_dag(data.frame(
  from = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
  to = c("b", "c", "d", "d")
))
```

## Titles, captions and annotations

```{r}
#| label: title
#| fig-alt: "The graph with a title and subtitle added."
ggplot_dag(dag) + labs(title = "A small pipeline", subtitle = "four targets")
```

```{r}
#| label: caption
#| fig-alt: "The graph with a caption added below it."
ggplot_dag(dag) + labs(caption = "Generated with ggtargets")
```

```{r}
#| label: annotate
#| fig-alt: "The graph with a text annotation pointing out a specific node."
lay <- dag_layout(dag, style_metro())
node_d <- lay$nodes[lay$nodes$name == "d", ]
ggplot_dag(dag) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = node_d$x + 30,
    y = node_d$y,
    label = "merge point",
    hjust = 0,
    color = "gray30",
    size = 3
  )
```

## Highlighting a path

`edge_paths` (in a `dag_layout`) has one full point-path per graph edge - `from`/`to`/`piece`/`x`/`y`/`order` - even where the default drawing shares one line across several edges. Filter it to the edges on a path of interest, sort each edge's points by `order` (their order along the path), and layer it on top of the base plot to trace that path without disturbing anything else:

```{r}
#| label: highlight
#| fig-alt: "The graph with the a-to-c-to-d path traced in a thick red highlight over the base plot."
path_edges <- data.frame(from = c("a", "c"), to = c("c", "d"))
highlight <- merge(lay$edge_paths, path_edges)
ord <- order(paste(highlight$from, highlight$to), highlight$order)
highlight <- highlight[ord, ]

ggplot_dag(dag) +
  geom_path(
    data = highlight,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = paste(from, to)),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.5
  )
```

Highlighting more than one path at once works the same way - give each its own subset and color:

```{r}
#| label: highlight2
#| fig-alt: "The graph with two paths highlighted in different colors: a-to-c-to-d in red, a-to-b-to-d in blue."
path1 <- merge(lay$edge_paths, data.frame(from = c("a", "c"), to = c("c", "d")))
path2 <- merge(lay$edge_paths, data.frame(from = c("a", "b"), to = c("b", "d")))
path1 <- path1[order(paste(path1$from, path1$to), path1$order), ]
path2 <- path2[order(paste(path2$from, path2$to), path2$order), ]

ggplot_dag(dag) +
  geom_path(
    data = path1,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = paste(from, to)),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_path(
    data = path2,
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = paste(from, to)),
    color = "blue",
    linewidth = 1.5,
    alpha = 0.5
  )
```

## Building the plot layer by layer

`dag_layers()` returns the layers alone, for full manual assembly - useful for inserting a custom layer *between* ggtargets' own layers (here, a background rectangle drawn before the nodes but after the edges):

```{r}
#| label: manual
#| fig-alt: "The graph manually assembled from dag_layers(), with a shaded rectangle inserted between the edge and node layers."
layers <- dag_layers(lay)
is_node_layer <- vapply(
  layers,
  function(l) {
    inherits(l, "Layer") && inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint")
  },
  logical(1)
)
first_node <- which(is_node_layer)[1]

ggplot() +
  layers[seq_len(first_node - 1)] +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = -Inf,
    xmax = Inf,
    ymin = 40,
    ymax = 60,
    fill = "khaki",
    alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  layers[seq(first_node, length(layers))] +
  dag_theme()
```

## Combining plots with patchwork

Two ggtargets plots (or a ggtargets plot and any other ggplot) combine like any other patchwork layout. Patchwork does its own panel layout, so use `fixed_size = FALSE` and let it size the panels:

```{r}
#| label: patchwork
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-alt: "Two versions of the graph, default and status-colored, side by side."
dag2 <- as_dag(
  data.frame(from = c("a", "a", "b", "c"), to = c("b", "c", "d", "d")),
  nodes = data.frame(
    name = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
    status = c("uptodate", "outdated", "errored", "queued")
  )
)
p1 <- ggplot_dag(dag, fixed_size = FALSE) + labs(title = "default")
p2 <- ggplot_dag(
  dag2,
  node_color = "status",
  palette = targets_status_colors(),
  fixed_size = FALSE
) +
  labs(title = "by status")
patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)
```

## Overriding the theme

The plot's theme (added by `dag_theme()`) is an ordinary ggplot2 theme, so any of its elements can be overridden afterwards - here, a legend moved to the bottom and set on a shaded panel background:

```{r}
#| label: theme-override
#| fig-alt: "The status-colored graph with its legend moved to the bottom and a shaded gray panel background."
ggplot_dag(dag2, node_color = "status", palette = targets_status_colors()) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.background = element_rect(
      fill = "gray95",
      color = NA
    )
  )
```

## Exporting at different sizes

`ggplot_dag()` gives the panel a fixed physical size: one data unit is `zoom` pixels at 96 dpi. Element sizes therefore stay the same across graphs. `dag_size()` returns the whole plot's size in inches, legend and titles included, and `ggsave_dag()` saves at that size. Its `scale` argument raises resolution (`dpi`), not physical size. `zoom` changes the physical size, scaling nodes, lines and text together. `ggplot2::ggsave()` works too, as long as you pass it `dag_size()`'s width and height:

```{r}
#| label: export
p <- ggplot_dag(dag)
dag_size(p)

# true pixel size
ggsave_dag(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), p)
# 3x resolution, same proportions
ggsave_dag(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), p, scale = 3)
# twice as large
ggsave_dag(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), ggplot_dag(dag, zoom = 2))
```

Adding a *complete* theme, such as `+ theme_void()`, replaces the fixed panel size, and the plot stretches to the device again. Override individual `theme()` elements instead, as above.
